{{About|the euphemism for the play ''[[Macbeth]]''|other plays|The Scottish Play (Lee Blessing play){{!}}''The Scottish Play'' (Lee Blessing play)|and|The Scottish Play (Graham Holliday play){{!}}''The Scottish Play'' (Graham Holliday play)|Scottish plays in general|Scottish literature}}

[[File:A traxedia de Macbeth 1972 Shakespeare.jpg|thumb|A 1972 book cover for a [[Galician language|Galician]] printing of ''[[Macbeth]]''. [[theatrical superstitions|Theatrical superstition]] holds that speaking the name ''Macbeth'' inside a theatre will lead to a curse.]]

'''''The Scottish Play''''' and '''''the Bard's play''''' are [[euphemism|euphemisms]] for the [[William Shakespeare]] play ''[[Macbeth]]''. The first is a reference to the play's [[Scotland|Scottish]] setting, and the second is a reference to Shakespeare's popular [[nickname]]. According to a [[theatrical superstitions|theatrical superstition]], called the ''Scottish [[curse]]'', speaking the name ''Macbeth'' inside a theatre, other than as called for in the script while rehearsing or performing, will cause disaster. On top of the aforementioned alternative titles, some people also refer to the classical tragedy as ''Mackers'' for this reason. Variations of the superstition may also forbid quoting lines from the play within a theatre except as part of an actual rehearsal or performance of the play.

Because of this superstition, the [[Macbeth (character)|title character]] is often referred to as the ''Scottish King'' or ''Scottish Lord''. [[Lady Macbeth]] is often referred to as the ''Scottish Lady'' or ''Lady M''. However, one of the most popular traditions among Shakespeare-specific actors allows "Macbeth" as a reference to the character. Nonetheless, many call the pair "Macb" and "Lady Macb".<ref>{{cite news|author=David Lyman|title=This show is so cursed, you can't even call it by name|url=https://www.cincinnati.com/story/entertainment/theater/2019/03/27/macbeth-superstitions-history-and-removal-scottish-curse/3288680002/}}</ref>

==Origins==
The traditional origin is said to be a curse set upon the play by a coven of [[witch|witches]], angry at Shakespeare for using a real spell.<ref name="rsc">{{cite web |title=The Curse of the Scottish Play |url=https://www.rsc.org.uk/macbeth/about-the-play/the-scottish-play |website=RSC.org.uk |publisher=Royal Shakespeare Company |access-date=8 October 2021}}</ref> One hypothesis for the origin of this superstition is that ''Macbeth'', being a popular play, was commonly put on by theatres in financial trouble, or that the high production costs of ''Macbeth'' put theatres in financial trouble. Hence, an association was made between productions of ''Macbeth'' and theatres going out of business.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Harrison |first=Martin |title=The Language of Theatre |publisher=Routeledge |year=1998 |page=239 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ofbGhtZyiHwC |isbn=0-87830-087-2}}</ref>

==Cleansing ritual==
When the name of the play is spoken in a theatre, tradition requires the person who spoke it to leave, perform traditional cleansing [[ritual|rituals]], and be invited back in. The rituals are supposed to ward off the evil that uttering the play's name is feared to bring on.

The rituals include turning three times, spitting over one's left shoulder, swearing, or reciting a line from another of Shakespeare's plays.<ref name="Garber">{{Cite book |last=Garber |first=Marjorie B. |author-link=Marjorie Garber |title=Shakespeare's Ghost Writers: Literature as Uncanny Causality |publisher=Methuen |year=1997 |page=88 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9EsYy1TZkUwC |isbn=0-416-09432-5}}</ref> Popular lines for this purpose include, "Angels and ministers of grace defend us" (''[[Hamlet]]'' 1.IV), "If we shadows have offended" (''[[A Midsummer Night's Dream]]'' 5.II), and "Fair thoughts and happy hours attend on you" (''[[The Merchant of Venice]]'', 3.IV).<ref name="Garber"/> A more elaborate cleansing ritual involves leaving the theatre, spinning around and brushing oneself off, and saying "Macbeth" three times before entering again. Some production groups insist that the offender may not re-enter the theatre until invited to do so, therefore making it easy to punish frequent offenders by leaving them outside.

A portrayal of the ritual occurs in the 1983 film ''[[The Dresser (1983 film)|The Dresser]]'', in which the lead character Sir is the offender, and his dresser Norman officiates over the propitiation.

The cleansing rituals have been parodied numerous times in popular culture, including in ''[[Blackadder]]'', ''[[Slings and Arrows]]'', ''[[The Simpsons]]'', ''[[The West Wing]]'', and ''[[Make It Pop]]''.<ref>{{cite book|author=Laurie Maguire and Emma Smith|title=30 Great Myths about Shakespeare|publisher=John Wiley & Sons|year=2012|page=151|isbn=978-1118324875}}</ref> For example, in the ''Blackadder'' episode "[[Sense and Senility]]", a parody ritual performed by two actors involves slapping each other's hands [[Pat-a-cake, pat-a-cake, baker's man#The game|pat-a-cake]] fashion, followed by tweaking the other person's nose. In ''Slings and Arrows'', a guest director mocks the superstition by saying "Macbeth" onstage. While spinning around, she falls off on her third spin, resulting in an injury that takes her out of commission for the rest of the season. On ''The Simpsons'', the core five are invited into a performance by [[Ian McKellen]] (in Scottish attire, clearly in the title role). The family keeps saying the title, which only makes more bad luck strike the actor, including lightning striking him and the "{{resize|94|MAC}}" falling from the signage (leaving the "{{resize|94|BETH}}").<ref>{{cite book|first=Richard|last=Burt|title=Shakespeares after Shakespeare: an encyclopedia of the Bard in mass media and popular culture, Volume 2|publisher=Greenwood Press|year=2007|page=698|isbn=978-0313331183}}</ref>

[[Patrick Stewart]], on the radio program ''[[Ask Me Another (radio program)|Ask Me Another]]'', asserted that "if you [[Macbeth (2010 film)|have played the role]] of the Scottish thane, then you are allowed to say the title, any time anywhere."<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.npr.org/2015/08/20/432887463/brush-up-your-shakespeare|title=Brush up Your Shakespeare|newspaper=NPR.org}}</ref>

==Historical mishaps==
English actor Harold Norman, playing Macbeth, was mortally wounded in a sword fight during a performance of ''Macbeth'' at Oldham's Colosseum Theatre on 30 January 1947. He was hospitalized and died three weeks later.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://trove.nla.gov.au/newspaper/article/42534070 |title=DIES AFTER STAGE BATTLE ACCIDENTALLY STABBED AS MACBETH. |newspaper=[[The Cairns Post]] |agency=[[Australian Associated Press|A.A.P.]] |at=Page 1, column 4 |date=28 February 1947 |issue=14,037 |access-date=10 June 2023 |via=[[Trove]]}}</ref>

On 2 December 1964, a fire burned down the [[D. Maria II National Theatre]] in Lisbon, Portugal. At the time, the play being shown was ''Macbeth''.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://150anos.dn.pt/2014/09/18/o-incendio-no-teatro-nacional-d-maria-ii/|title=O incêndio no Teatro Nacional D. Maria II {{!}} DN 150 Anos|access-date=1 July 2016|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161011034404/http://150anos.dn.pt/2014/09/18/o-incendio-no-teatro-nacional-d-maria-ii/|archive-date=11 October 2016}}</ref>

In 1980, a production of ''Macbeth'' at [[The Old Vic]] starring [[Peter O'Toole]], often referred to as ''Macdeath'', was performed. It was reviewed so badly that the [[Prospect Theatre Company]] disbanded shortly after the play.<ref>[[The Old Vic]]</ref>

Mishaps on the set of his film ''[[Opera (1987 film)|Opera]]'' led director [[Dario Argento]] to believe that the film had been affected by the Macbeth curse; the opera being performed within the film is [[Giuseppe Verdi]]'s ''[[Macbeth (Verdi)|Macbeth]]''.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0093677/reference|title=Opera (1987)|via=www.imdb.com}}</ref>{{Failed verification|date=May 2019}}

In 1988, Bulgarian singer, coach, and translator [[Bantcho Bantchevsky]] committed suicide while attending a nationally broadcast matinee of Verdi's ''Macbeth''. He propelled himself backward from a balcony railing at New York's [[Metropolitan Opera House (Lincoln Center)|Metropolitan Opera House]], Lincoln Square.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1988/01/24/nyregion/opera-patron-dies-in-plunge-from-a-balcony-at-the-met.html|title="Opera Patron Dies ... at the Met", The New York Times|newspaper=The New York Times|date=24 January 1988|last1=McFadden|first1=Robert D.}}</ref>

In 2014, during the filming of [[Justin Kurzel]]'s ''[[Macbeth (2015 film)|Macbeth]]'' (2015), the cast and crew began referring to it as "The Scottish Film" after a series of strange incidents happened on set. Kurzel said he tried to dismiss the superstition, however, a number of things happened on set that made him question the history of the play. Kurzel hoped the name change would improve their luck.<ref>{{Cite web |date=1 October 2015 |title=Macbeth directed by Justin Kurzel starring Michael Fassbender |url=https://thewest.com.au/entertainment/movies/kurzel-revisits-king-killer-tale-ng-ya-129863 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20261009223054/https://thewest.com.au/entertainment/movies/kurzel-revisits-king-killer-tale-ng-ya-129863 |archive-date=9 October 2026 |access-date=2026-10-10 |website=[[The West Australian]]}}</ref> While filming on the [[Isle of Skye]] under heavy rain, sleet and snow, some members of the cast suffered from [[hypothermia]],<ref>{{Cite news |date=28 September 2015 |title=Macbeth's Fassbender and Considine battered by Skye rain |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-scotland-highlands-islands-34378393 |work=[[BBC News]]}}</ref> and [[Marion Cotillard]] (who played Lady Macbeth) fell into a bog and submerged up to her neck. Kurzel said Cotillard disappeared, and for a moment he thought they had lost her.<ref name="Leigh">{{Cite news |last=Leigh |first=Danny |date=24 September 2015 |title=Macbeth director Justin Kurzel: ‘You’re getting close to evil’ |url=https://www.theguardian.com/film/2015/sep/24/macbeth-director-justin-kurzel-australian-film-maker-snowtown |work=[[The Guardian]] |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref> It took two crew members to pull Cotillard out as her feet sank into the mud.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Collin |first=Robbie |date=4 October 2015 |title='I never think I've delivered' - Michael Fassbender talks Macbeth and Hollywood highs and lows |url=https://www.independent.ie/entertainment/movies/i-never-think-ive-delivered-michael-fassbender-talks-macbeth-and-hollywood-highs-and-lows/a/150817676.html |website=[[Irish Independent]]}}</ref> Kurzel said that filming ''Macbeth'' felt like playing with a [[Ouija]] board. "After 18 takes of Marion doing "Come you spirits..." the atmosphere gets pretty weird. Once you start invoking certain things, it is like you're getting close to...evil, really."<ref name="Leigh"/> Kurzel said that there was "a supernatural element to filming in Skye in January, it seemed to be a place where spirits walk".<ref>{{Cite news |date=25 May 2015 |title=Fassbender tackles 'the Scottish film' |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/entertainment-arts-32850670 |work=BBC News |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20261009223025/https://www.bbc.com/news/entertainment-arts-32850670 |archive-date=9 October 2026 |access-date=10 October 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref>

[[Ari Aster]], writer and director of ''[[Hereditary (film)|Hereditary]]'' (2018), said that during filming, "[[Alex Wolff]] told me not to say the name of William Shakespeare's Scottish play out loud because of some superstitious theater legend. I smugly announced the name, and then one of our lights burst during the shooting of the following scene."<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.reddit.com/r/movies/comments/8rbjj7/hi_im_ari_aster_writerdirector_of_hereditary_ama/e0q4lcv/|title=Ari Aster comments on Shakespeare's Scottish Play curse|date=15 June 2018}}</ref>

In 2022, at the [[94th Academy Awards]], [[Chris Rock]] congratulated [[Denzel Washington]] on his performance in ''[[The Tragedy of Macbeth (2021 film)|The Tragedy of Macbeth]]'', saying the name of the Scottish play aloud in the [[Dolby Theatre]]. Moments later, [[Chris Rock–Will Smith slapping incident|Rock was slapped]] by [[Will Smith]] after making a joke implied to be about the alopecia that Smith's wife, [[Jada Pinkett Smith]], was struggling with at the time. Viewers, including playwright [[Lynn Nottage]], quickly took to social media to joke that Rock had suffered the curse of the Scottish play.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.townandcountrymag.com/leisure/arts-and-culture/a39561240/will-smith-chris-rock-oscars-twitter-reaction-macbeth/|title=Former Theater Kids Everywhere Had the Same Reaction to Will Smith Hitting Chris Rock|date=28 March 2022}}</ref>

Further instances include the [[Astor Place Riot]] in 1849, injuries sustained by actors at a 1937 performance at The Old Vic that starred [[Laurence Olivier]], [[Diana Wynyard]]'s accidental fall in 1948, and burns suffered by [[Charlton Heston]] in 1954.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.sfgate.com/performance/article/Cal-Shakes-risks-curse-of-the-Scottish-play-3255547.php|title=Cal Shakes risks curse of 'the Scottish play'|last=Hurwitt|first=Robert|newspaper=[[San Francisco Chronicle]]|date=19 August 2010|access-date=10 September 2015}}</ref>

[[Petersham, New South Wales|Petersham]], [[Lewisham, New South Wales|Lewisham]], [[Haberfield, New South Wales|Haberfield]], [[Summer Hill, New South Wales|Summer Hill]] [[Ashfield, New South Wales|Ashfield]]. [[Five Dock]], [[Croydon, New South Wales|Croydon]], [[Concord, New South Wales|Concord]], [[Burwood, New South Wales|Burwood]], [[Strathfield]], [[Homebush]], [[Auburn, New South Wales|Auburn]]}} '''Parramatta Road''' is the major historical east-west artery of metropolitan [[Sydney]], [[New South Wales]], Australia, connecting the [[Sydney central business district|Sydney CBD]] with [[Parramatta]]. It is the easternmost part of the [[Great Western Highway]]. Since the 1990s its role has been augmented by the [[City West Link]] and [[M4 Motorway (Sydney)|M4 Motorway]]. The road begins in the east as a continuation of [[George Street, Sydney|George Street]], which becomes [[Broadway, New South Wales|Broadway]] west of [[Harris Street]], and Parramatta Road west of the [[City Road, Sydney|City Road]] junction, and ends at the junction with Church Street in Parramatta. Its {{convert|23|km|mi|0}} distance is dominated by caryards and small marginally-viable shops. At the same time, however, it has over 100 [[ghost town|abandoned]] and derelict stores.{{cite web|url=http://www.dailytelegraph.com.au/citys-main-artery-a-desolate-wasteland/story-fn6e0s1g-1226040627972|publisher=[[Daily Telegraph (Sydney)|The Daily Telegraph]]| title = City's main artery a desolate wasteland |date= 18 April 2011 |access-date=14 January 2015}}{{cite web |url=http://www.au.timeout.com/sydney/film/venues/5644/av-union |publisher=Time Out Sydney, Nicholas Adams |title=AV Union |date=16 October 2012 |access-date=14 January 2015 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150115081557/http://www.au.timeout.com/sydney/film/venues/5644/av-union |archive-date=15 January 2015 }} Owing to this and its abrasively noisy traffic, it has rarely been considered beautiful.{{cite web|url=http://www.altmedia.net.au/renew-project-targets-forum/84234|publisher= Alt Media, Mason McCann | title = Renew project targets Forum |date= 26 September 2013 |access-date=14 January 2015}} Opened in 1811, it is one of Sydney's oldest roads and Australia's first road between two cities (before Sydney and Parramatta coalesced). As at 2015, over three million commuters every year drove Parramatta Road.{{cite web |url=http://www.parramattaroad.com/html/history.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150115075854/http://www.parramattaroad.com/html/history.html |archive-date=15 January 2015 |title=PARRAMATTA ROAD – History}} The road is the hub of Sydney's motor dealership industry - with 67% of the adjacent land used for motor retailing and services. ==History== ===1790s–1800s: Development=== [[File:Parramattard1870susyd.jpg|thumb|left|200px|A carriage marked "Ashfield-Burwood" trundles down Parramatta Road in the early 1870s, with the [[University of Sydney]] in the background.]] British settlement in [[Parramatta]] began in the same year (1788) as it did in Sydney. The [[Parramatta River]] was used as navigation between them. Sometime between 1789 and 1791 an overland track was made to provide an official land route between the two settlements.{{Citation|author1=Broomham, Rosemary|title=Vital connections: a history of NSW roads from 1788|date=2001|publisher=Hale & Iremonger in association with the [[Roads & Traffic Authority]]|isbn=978-0-86806-703-2|page=25}} Parramatta Road dates to the 1792 formation of a route linking Sydney to the settlement of Parramatta. This route was formalised under the direction of [[Surveyor-General of New South Wales|Surveyor–General]] [[Augustus Alt]] in 1797. Parramatta Road became one of the [[Colonial Australia|colony's]] most important early roads, and for many years remained one of Sydney's principal thoroughfares.{{cite web|url=http://141.243.32.146/heritageapp/ViewHeritageItemDetails.aspx?ID=4310580|title=Sandstone Kerb - Parramatta Road|work=State Heritage Register|publisher=[[Office of Environment & Heritage]], [[Government of New South Wales]]|year=2005|access-date=7 October 2013}} The early road was a poorly built and poorly maintained track through bush. In 1794, the governor of the colony reported that he had caused a very good road to be made, but there is no evidence that any bridges were built over the streams. The road subsequently deteriorated and on 9 June 1805 the ''Sydney Gazette'' reported that the road was impassable as the result of heavy rain. Attempts to improve the road continued over the years.Francis Peron, 'Account of Port Jackson and Sydney Town, New South Wales', translation quoted in The literary panorama, vol 10, Charles Taylor, London, 1809, col 921 ===1810–1815=== By 1811, Parramatta Road had officially opened to traffic and was financed during a large portion of the 19th century by a [[toll road|toll]], with toll booths located at what now is [[University of Sydney|Sydney University]] and the [[Duck River (New South Wales)|Duck River]]. [[Lachlan Macquarie|Governor Macquarie]] called tenders for the repair of the road, raised a three [[shilling]] per gallon levy on spirits and levied a toll to pay for the work. The road was to be 10 metres wide. This turnpike road was opened on 10 April 1811. The toll barriers were at the present [[Railway Square]] and at Becket's Creek (near Parramatta).{{citation needed|date=March 2019}} In 1814, a stage cart service was established along Parramatta Road. Fares were 10 shillings for passengers and 3 pence for letters. Heavy rain again nearly destroyed this road, so in 1817 it was announced that all tree-stumps would be removed and the road paved with stone which would be covered with earth and gravel. This improvement was announced as finished on 15 January 1815.{{citation needed|date=March 2019}} In 1815 the "profit" from the Sydney toll reached £465. The growth of Sydney caused the toll barrier to be moved to Grose Farm (present University of Sydney) in April 1836. In 1839 it was moved further west to [[Annandale, New South Wales|Annandale]].{{citation needed|date=March 2019}} ===1820s–1880s=== [[Image:ParramattaRd1938.jpg|left|thumb|200px|Parramatta Road in the 1930s looking east across [[Iron Cove Creek]] towards [[Lewisham, New South Wales|Lewisham]]]] The colony's first stage coach (valued at £300) was imported in 1821 but did not begin regular service until 1823. The stage left the city at 7:00 am, arrived in Parramatta at 9:30 am and left Parramatta for the return journey at 4:00 pm. Inside passengers were charged six shillings. Hazards on the road included the threat of attacks by Indigenous people and bushrangers. Hotels and settlements sprang up along the road to serve coaching traffic.The Roadmakers: A History of Main Roads in New South Wales, [[Department of Main Roads (New South Wales)|Department of Main Roads]], Sydney, 1976, p 47 The importance of the road declined with the advent of the [[Main Suburban railway line|Sydney-Parramatta railway]] in 1855. In 1883, a steam tram line opened along Parramatta Road as far as Annandale, and was extended onward to [[Norton Street]] in 1884, where it turned to run along Norton Street to Short Street. In the 1800s, the government acquired a strip of land from [[Ashfield, New South Wales|Ashfield]] to [[Burwood, New South Wales|Burwood]] from the Rosebank Estate, owned by the [[Sisters of the Good Samaritan]], Australia's first religious congregation. [[Rosebank College]] now stands on the former Rosebank Estate, and the heritage-listed building of the private school stands adjacent to the road at [[Five Dock]]. ===1900s–present: Motorisation=== Sydney Municipal Council began widening the major routes into the city centre in 1911, including the construction of [[Broadway, Sydney|Broadway]] and the widening of the cutting on Parramatta Road adjacent to Sydney University. In the 1920s, the road was sealed and [[Trams in Sydney|tramlines]] were removed from the road. Sheep and cattle were still crossing Parramatta Road at [[Homebush]] as late as the 1960s.{{cn|date=March 2026}} Increased traffic congestion along the road steadily made it less attractive for residential and commercial use during the 20th century. By the last quarter of the 20th century, the only active businesses on many stretches of the road were car dealerships. The decline of industry in the [[Inner West]] also drove the decline of commercial areas formerly catering to factory workers. By the end of the 20th{{nbsp}}century, proposals to revitalise Parramatta Road and make it more attractive were regularly made.{{cn|date=March 2026}} In 1985, the Design Arts Board of the Australia Council sponsored an ideas competition for Parramatta Road.{{cite report |title=Parramatta Road Urban Design Study and Guidelines |url=https://nswdpe.intersearch.com.au/nswdpejspui/handle/1/4286 |year=1986 |author=Department of Environment and Planning }} {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20261024154504/https://nswdpe.intersearch.com.au/nswdpejspui/bitstream/1/4286/1/Parramatta%20Road%20Urban%20Design%20Study%20and%20Guidelines.pdf |date=2026-10-24}} {{rp|at=p.1}} One of these proposals was made in 2012, which would have widened and lowered the road below street level in a "slot" as part of the [[Roads & Maritime Services]] [[WestConnex]] motorway proposal. This plan was abandoned, and the WestConnex proposal was later changed to a pair of tunnels parallel to Parramatta Road and connecting to the existing M4 motorway. The new extension was known as [[M4 Motorway (Sydney)|M4 East]] and was eventually built between the end of the existing M4 motorway in [[North Strathfield]] and [[Haberfield, New South Wales|Haberfield]], where it connected to the A4 road. The new tunnels opened to traffic in July 2019.{{cite web|url=https://www.nsw.gov.au/improving-nsw/infrastructure-projects/westconnex/|title=WestConnex|website=NSW Government|access-date=10 July 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190710072445/https://www.nsw.gov.au/improving-nsw/infrastructure-projects/westconnex/|archive-date=10 July 2019|url-status=live}}{{cite web|url=https://www.westconnex.com.au/news-media/new-m4-tunnels-open-weekend|title=New M4 tunnels to open this weekend|publisher=[[WestConnex]]|date=10 July 2019|access-date=10 July 2019|archive-date=10 July 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190710073104/https://www.westconnex.com.au/news-media/new-m4-tunnels-open-weekend|url-status=dead}} The project resulted in the creation of a new entry and exit ramp on Parramatta Road in Ashfield, the narrowing of westbound traffic lanes for through-traffic to one lane at either end of the tunnel, and the demolition of a large number of houses in Ashfield and Haberfield to make way for the tunnel ramps. ==Criticism== [[File:Homebush_Cinema.JPG|thumb|200px|Homebush Cinema, built in 1925, is one of the many derelict establishments on the road, which operated until 1996 as a [[party|reception]] centre.]] The road has been criticised by the community for its traffic [[pollution]], [[Traffic congestion|congestion]], and for its vacant shops and [[modern ruins|rundown buildings]], particularly between [[Leichhardt, New South Wales|Leichhardt]] and [[Concord, New South Wales|Concord]], and local government has been accused of failing to adopt policies to encourage the redevelopment and regeneration of vacant sites.{{cite web|url=http://www.ciaomagazine.com.au/can-parramatta-rd-rock/|publisher= Ciao Magazine | title = CAN PARRAMATTA RD ROCK ONCE MORE? |date= 12 July 2013 |access-date=14 January 2015}} A local mayor described it as a "varicose vein".{{cite web|url=http://www.smh.com.au/nsw/its-official-parramatta-road-will-get-60000-new-apartments-by-2050-20141122-11rsmg.html |publisher=[[Sydney Morning Herald]]| title = 200-year dream for renewal and free flow for 'varicose vein' |date= 5 Oct 2012|access-date=16 January 2015}} A NSW Business Chamber Executive [[Patricia Forsythe]] said that the road is "one of the least attractive commercial areas of Sydney". Former NSW premier [[Nick Greiner]] thought the road looked "like [[Beirut]] on a bad day". ''[[The Sydney Morning Herald]]'' writer [[Elizabeth Farrelly]] described it as "filthy, noisy, sclerotic and dull".{{cite web|url=http://www.smh.com.au/federal-politics/political-opinion/developers-wont-save-parramatta-road-alone-20120620-20oes.html |publisher=[[The Sydney Morning Herald]] | title =Developers won't save Parramatta Road alone |date= 21 June 2012|access-date=16 January 2015}} On a lighter note, Tess De Quincey, an Australian performer and director said, "Every chapter of Sydney's history has been written on Parramatta Road."{{cite web |url=https://books.google.com/books?isbn=9052010366 |title = isbn:9052010366 – Google Search}} A Sydney Morning Herald editor said that whilst the road is "ugly in parts, drab in others, and generally unpleasant", it is still "fundamental to the economic and social viability of the [[Greater Western Sydney|greater city]]".{{cite web|url=http://www.smh.com.au/comment/smh-editorial/a-chance-to-get-parramatta-road-right-20141030-11ee3x.html|publisher= Sydney Morning Herald | title =A chance to get Parramatta Road right |date= 31 Oct 2014|access-date=16 January 2015}} Since the 1970s many buildings fronting Parramatta Road, especially those in the prime locations of the [[Inner West]] (from [[Newtown, New South Wales|Newtown]] to [[Homebush]]), have become vacant and fallen into disrepair, with many [[vandalise]]d. Previously these buildings were a major part of local life for the suburbs along Parramatta Road, providing employment, retailing and other services. The buildings with [[graffiti]] and broken windows provide a sight that is sought out by [[Urban exploration|graffiti vandals and proficient urban photographers]].[https://www.dailytelegraph.com.au/business/why-derelict-buildings-worth-millions-are-being-left-behind-in-a-region-desperate-for-places-to-live/news-story/6cb0b9b9701cfdfb8205f9c02a161439 Why derelict buildings worth millions are being left behind in a region desperate for places to live] by David Barwell ([[Daily Telegraph (Sydney)|The Daily Telegraph]]) Nicholas Munning, an owner of a [[music store]] in [[Annandale, New South Wales|Annandale]], described the road as, "A lost cause...You can see the hodgepodge of buildings - abandoned buildings, abandoned shops - [with people thinking] let's just let this sit here for four years until we get council approval to knock it down and build apartments...They don't care if it sits there vacant with broken windows and looks like shit, The problem is the whole road looks like that. So nobody is going to say, 'hey, this is a great area. I'm going to spend $x making a really classy looking shop or restaurant'."[https://www.smh.com.au/national/nsw/the-shops-have-closed-parramatta-road-a-lost-cause-retailer-says-20180807-p4zw29.html 'The shops have closed': Parramatta Road 'a lost cause', retailer says] by Garry Maddox (''[[The Sydney Morning Herald]]'') == Redevelopment plans == There have been at least five recent plans to transform Parramatta Road, including "1996 Parramatta Road: Beyond 2000"{{r|latestPlanBowring2024}}{{cite news |url=https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/article/2024/jul/27/boulevard-of-broken-dreams-could-parramatta-rd-really-become-sydneys-champs-elysees |author=Elias Visontay |work=[[The Guardian]] |date=2024-07-27 |title='Boulevard of broken dreams': could Parramatta Road really become Sydney's Champs-Élysées? |quote=Another plan in 1996, “Parramatta Road – Beyond 2000”, which included a taskforce that proposed more trees and bike paths to revitalise sections but without a solution to remove the traffic, did not materialise. In 2004, another plan was put forward, centred on new homes and jobs along the corridor. }}, 1996 ''Parramatta Road 2000 and Beyond''{{cite report |title=Parramatta Road 2000 and Beyond - A STRATEGIC FRAMEWORK TO REVITALISE PARRAMATTA ROAD |publisher=Parramatta Road 2000 and Beyond Steering Committee, IMROC |author1=Inner Metropolitan Regional Organisation of Councils |author2=John Sharpe |author3=Cleveland Rose |author4=Chris Elliott |isbn=095855420X |id=L007833;981091 |date=October 1998 }}
{{cite book |isbn=095855420X |year=1998 |url=https://archives.cityofsydney.nsw.gov.au/nodes/view/1753799 |title=Parramatta Road 2000 and beyond: a strategic framework to revitalise Parramatta Road |publisher=[[City of Sydney]] |id=LIB-00016695 }} {{Cite AV media/old |author=JANE GOODALL |publisher=ABC |program=Radio National Breakfast |title=parra b/gnd |date=2000-05-10 |url=https://www.abc.net.au/listen/programs/radionational-breakfast/parra-bgnd/3466682 |quote=In Oct 1997, 12 councils along the road, the RTA and a number of other interested parties, environment/transport groups formed a partnership with IMROC - Inner Metropolitan regional organisation of councils - to develop projects to revitalise Parramatta Raod. }}, 1998 "2000 Clover Moore's Parramatta Road Taskforce", the "2011 NRMA re-imagining" and "2016 Inner West Council".{{cite web |url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/2024-07-24/john-graham-reveals-approach-fixin-parramatta-road-sydney/104133872 |title=Parramatta Road's latest future plan to be revealed in roads minister's speech at Committee for Sydney summit |date=2024-07-24 |first=Declan |last=Bowring |publisher=[[ABC News (Australia)|ABC News]] }} The [[Government of New South Wales]] published the 'Parramatta Road Urban Transformation Strategy' in 2016, with a 30{{nbsp}}year plan for redeveloping the area through planning and infrastructure investment.{{Cite web|date=2020-02-19|title=Parramatta Road Urban Transformation Strategy 2016|url=https://www.landcom.com.au/organisation/publications/parramatta-road-urban-transformation-strategy-2016/|access-date=2021-03-11|website=Landcom|language=en-AU}} Among the strategy's goals are housing an additional 56,000 people in 27,000 new homes on the corridor (with minimum five percent [[affordable housing]]); 50,000 workers employed in the area; and 66 [[hectare]]s of new open space is provided through [[linear park]]s and along watercourses or infrastructure.{{Cite web|title=Parramatta Road Corridor Urban Transformation Strategy|url=https://www.landcom.com.au/assets/Publications/Parramatta/ed08175423/parramatta-road-transformation-strategy-report.pdf}} The proposed development rights are worth millions of dollars to [[Real estate development|developers]] but are also controversial due to the density of some of the proposals and the likely impact on an already over-congested road. As a result, many of the development proposals are controversial with local residents and are opposed by local councils. A number of the disputes between developers and councils have led to court disputes. [[The Sydney Morning Herald]] reported plans developed for [[Transport for NSW]] between the [[Sydney central business district|Sydney CBD]] and [[Burwood, New South Wales|Burwood]] were abandoned in the months in the first three months of 2017. The project was estimated to cost up to $2.7 billion.{{Cite web |last=Saulwick |first=Jacob |date=2017-07-20 |title=Parramatta Road tram plans developed - then scrapped |url=https://www.smh.com.au/national/nsw/parramatta-road-tram-plans-developed--then-scrapped-20170720-gxfb1p.html |access-date=2026-11-10 |website=The Sydney Morning Herald |language=en}} A document repapered for a risk workshop found the bus network would not be able to accommodate planned growth.{{Cite report |url=https://www.smh.com.au/cqstatic/gxf5j4/lighrraildesign.pdf |title=lighrraildesign.pdf |date= |year=2017 |publisher=[[Transport for NSW]] |via=[[The Sydney Morning Herald]] |url-status=dead}} Block-by-block designs were published{{Cite report |url=http://www.smh.com.au/cqstatic/gxfd47/Light%20Rail%20Drawings.pdf |title=Light Rail Drawings.pdf |date= |publisher=[[The Sydney Morning Herald]] |publication-date=2017}} and documents marked [[Cabinet collective responsibility|cabinet-in-confidence]]{{Cite report |url=http://www.smh.com.au/cqstatic/gxfctc/LightRailImplementation1.pdf |title=LightRailImplementation1.pdf |date= |year=2017 |publisher=[[Transport for NSW]] |via=[[The Sydney Morning Herald]] |url-status=dead}}{{Cite report |url=http://www.smh.com.au/cqstatic/gxf5ha/LightRailRisk1.pdf |title=Parramatta Road Intermediate Transit - Risk Workshop |date=2016-11-03 |publisher=[[Transport for NSW]] |via=[[The Sydney Morning Herald]]|url-status=dead|archive-url=http://web.archive.org/web/20191213221523/https://www.smh.com.au/cqstatic/gxf5ha/LightRailRisk1.pdf|pages=4,6,7,8,10|archive-date=2019-12-13}} were published. The [[Inner West Council]] and [[City of Canada Bay]], through which the road runs for much of its length, have proposed using an electric [[guided bus]] running on the centre of the road for public transport, as opposed to kerbside buses as suggested in the strategy.{{Cite web|title=Parramatta Road Urban Renewal - Inner West Council|url=https://www.innerwest.nsw.gov.au/develop/works-and-projects/state-government-projects/parramatta-road-urban-renewal|access-date=2021-03-11|website=www.innerwest.nsw.gov.au}} ALTRAC Light Rail have proposed that a [[light rail]] corridor between Parramatta Road and [[Green Square, New South Wales|Green Square]] be developed.{{cite web |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250419115829/https://altraclightrail.com.au/proposal/ |url=https://altraclightrail.com.au/proposal/ |access-date=16 March 2026 |archive-date=19 April 2025 |url-status=live |title=Parramatta Road to Green Square – The next stage of Sydney's Light Rail |publisher=ALTRAC Light Rail}} In October 2025, Burwood Council proposed a light rail plan.{{cite news |title=Calls for Parramatta Road light rail corridor to unlock 100,000 homes from Central to Burwood |url=https://www.dailytelegraph.com.au/news/nsw/calls-for-parramatta-road-light-rail-corridor-to-unlock-100000-homes-from-central-to-burwood/news-story/4bc67e6e1f73166da561a9028a6d28ae |author=Peter Jenkins |publisher=Daily Telegraph |date=2026-10-28 }}{{cite report |url=https://burwood.infocouncil.biz/Open/2026/10/CM_27102026_AGN_AT.PDF |title=(Item MM18/26) Progressing a Light Rail Vision for Parramatta Road Through an Unsolicited Proposal |page=5 |publisher=Burwood Council }} ==Location== [[File:Parramatta Road at Burwood.JPG|thumb|right|200px|Parramatta Road looking west at Burwood, near [[Rosebank College]], during peak hour]] The highway forms the boundaries of various suburbs along the way and ends at the junction of Church Street, Parramatta, where the Great Western Highway briefly turns to the north. [[File:James Bateman.jpg|thumb|James Bateman]]
'''James Bateman''' (18 July 1811 – 27 November 1897) was a British landowner and [[horticulturist]]. He developed [[Biddulph Grange]] after moving there around 1840, from nearby [[Knypersley Hall]] in Staffordshire, England. He created the gardens at Biddulph with the aid of his wife Maria and his friend and painter of seascapes [[Edward William Cooke]].  From 1865 to 1870 he was the founding president of the [[North Staffordshire Field Club]], an organisation which researched local natural history and folklore.

== Biography ==

[[File:Biddulph Grange Gardens 02.jpg|thumb|His home [[Biddulph Grange]] and gardens in Staffordshire]]

[[File:Cycnoches egertonianum - Bateman Orch. Mex. Guat. pl. 40 (1842).jpg|thumb|Drawing of ''[[Cycnoches]] egertonianum'' by [[Sarah Drake]], from ''Orchidaceae of Mexico and Guatemala'', 1845]]

James Bateman was born at [[Redvales]] near [[Bury, Greater Manchester|Bury]] in Lancashire. He matriculated at [[Lincoln College, Oxford]], in 1829, graduating from [[Magdalen College, Oxford|Magdalen College]] with a BA in 1834 and an [[Master of Arts (Oxbridge)|MA]] in 1845. Over the next twenty years he made a great deal of money in iron, engineering and banking.<ref name="Lankesteriana">{{Cite journal|author=Lankester Botanical Garden |year=2010 |title=Biographies |journal=Lankesteriana |volume=10 |issue=2/3 |pages=183–206, page 183 |url=http://lankesteriana.org/lankesteriana/LANKESTERIANA%2010(2-3)/Lankesteriana%2010(2-3)%20Part%2010%20-%20Biographies.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140523220801/http://lankesteriana.org/lankesteriana/LANKESTERIANA%2010%282-3%29/Lankesteriana%2010%282-3%29%20Part%2010%20-%20Biographies.pdf |archive-date=23 May 2014 |url-status=live }}</ref>
In 1871, Bateman and his sons (who included the painter [[Robert Bateman (artist)|Robert Bateman]]) gave up the house and gardens at Biddulph, and he moved to [[Kensington]] in London. He later moved to [[Worthing]] in Sussex, where he died on 27 November 1897.{{sfn|Carlyle|1901}}

===Collector of plants===
"MA Magdalen College, Oxford, 1845, took great interest in collecting and cultivating tropical plants; FLS, 1833; FRS, 1838; fellow of Royal Horticultural Society; published writings on orchids and other horticultural subjects."<ref>''Concise Dictionary of National Biography,'' Oxford, 1995, p.169</ref>

He was a collector and scholar of [[orchids]], President of the North Staffordshire Field Society, and served on the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s Plant Exploration Committee.  He especially loved [[rhododendron]]s and [[azalea]]s. He had a number of sons who grew up at Biddulph Grange, including the painter [[Robert Bateman (artist)|Robert Bateman]].

The naturalist, Charles Darwin "received a box of orchids from Bateman on 25 January 1862 (and) a letter from him dated 28 January 1862."<ref name="Darwin">[http://www.darwinproject.ac.uk/darwinletters/calendar/entry-3356.html Darwin Correspondence Project – Letter 3356 — Bateman, James to Darwin, C. R., [1862]<!-- Bot generated title -->]. {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070927065916/http://www.darwinproject.ac.uk/darwinletters/calendar/entry-3356.html |date=27 September 2007 }}</ref>

===Garden designer===

Bateman created the gardens at Biddulph with the aid of his botanist wife Maria and his friend and painter of seascapes [[Edward William Cooke]].<ref>{{Cite book|last=Horwood|first=Catherine|title=Gardening Women: Their Stories From 1600 to the Present|publisher=Hachette, UK|year=2010|isbn=978-0748118335|location=United Kingdom|pages=94–95}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last=Musgrave|first=Toby|title=Seven deadly sins of gardening : and the vices and virtues of gardeners|last2=Calnan|first2=Mike|publisher=National Trust|year=2006|isbn=978-1-905400-46-1|location=London|pages=127–130|oclc=70173987}}</ref> His gardens at Biddulph are a rare survival of the interim period between [[Capability Brown]] [[landscape garden]] and the High [[Victorian era|Victorian]] style. The gardens are compartmentalised and divided into themes.

He "was also responsible for laying out the Arboretum at [[Derby]], the first public park in England."<ref>[http://www.francisfrith.com/search/england/staffordshire/biddulph/biddulph.htm Biddulph photos, maps, books, memories – Francis Frith] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070926231205/http://www.francisfrith.com/search/england/staffordshire/biddulph/biddulph.htm |date=26 September 2007 }}</ref>

=== Geology and religion ===

{{main|Geological Gallery, Biddulph Grange}}

[[File:The Geological Gallery, Biddulph Grange.jpg|thumb|center|upright=1.5<!--fmt for low img-->|The [[Geological Gallery, Biddulph Grange]], from the door. The bays represent the six days of [[biblical creation]].]]

Bateman expressed his strong religious beliefs in the [[Geological Gallery, Biddulph Grange|Geological Gallery at Biddulph Grange]]. Realising that a long sequence of rocks and fossils implied a great expanse of time before the supposed date of the creation of the world, he opened the gallery, a long straight corridor with specimens from oldest to youngest in sequence, to set out his view that the rocks were created by God in six days.<ref>{{cite web |title=Biddulph Grange Gardens |url=https://www.congleton-tc.gov.uk/attraction/biddulph-grange-gardens/ |publisher=Congleton Town Council |access-date=9 November 2026}}</ref><ref name="Historic England">{{cite web |title=Geological Gallery & (Site of) Orangery, Biddulph Grange |url=https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/heritage-gateway/results/record/c30a9cd9-4500-41f0-acda-ed2a4d72a681/MNA183731 |publisher=[[Historic England]] |id=MNA183731 |access-date=9 November 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Things to see in Biddulph Grange Garden: Geological Gallery |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/visit/shropshire-staffordshire/biddulph-grange-garden/things-to-see-at-biddulph-grange-garden#rt-geological-gallery |publisher=[[National Trust]] |access-date=10 November 2026}}</ref>

===Family===
On 24 April 1838, he married Maria Sybilla, third daughter of Rowland Egerton Warburton and sister of [[Peter Egerton Warburton]]; they had three sons, [[John Bateman (British politician)|John]], Rowland, and [[Robert Bateman (artist)|Robert]] (a notable painter), and a daughter, Katherine.{{sfn|Carlyle|1901}}

[[File:James Bateman.jpg|thumb|James Bateman]]
'''James Bateman''' (18 July 1811 – 27 November 1897) was a British landowner and [[horticulturist]]. He developed [[Biddulph Grange]] after moving there around 1840, from nearby [[Knypersley Hall]] in Staffordshire, England. He created the gardens at Biddulph with the aid of his wife Maria and his friend and painter of seascapes [[Edward William Cooke]].  From 1865 to 1870 he was the founding president of the [[North Staffordshire Field Club]], an organisation which researched local natural history and folklore.

== Biography ==

[[File:Biddulph Grange Gardens 02.jpg|thumb|His home [[Biddulph Grange]] and gardens in Staffordshire]]

[[File:Cycnoches egertonianum - Bateman Orch. Mex. Guat. pl. 40 (1842).jpg|thumb|Drawing of ''[[Cycnoches]] egertonianum'' by [[Sarah Drake]], from ''Orchidaceae of Mexico and Guatemala'', 1845]]

James Bateman was born at [[Redvales]] near [[Bury, Greater Manchester|Bury]] in Lancashire. He matriculated at [[Lincoln College, Oxford]], in 1829, graduating from [[Magdalen College, Oxford|Magdalen College]] with a BA in 1834 and an [[Master of Arts (Oxbridge)|MA]] in 1845. Over the next twenty years he made a great deal of money in iron, engineering and banking.<ref name="Lankesteriana">{{Cite journal|author=Lankester Botanical Garden |year=2010 |title=Biographies |journal=Lankesteriana |volume=10 |issue=2/3 |pages=183–206, page 183 |url=http://lankesteriana.org/lankesteriana/LANKESTERIANA%2010(2-3)/Lankesteriana%2010(2-3)%20Part%2010%20-%20Biographies.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140523220801/http://lankesteriana.org/lankesteriana/LANKESTERIANA%2010%282-3%29/Lankesteriana%2010%282-3%29%20Part%2010%20-%20Biographies.pdf |archive-date=23 May 2014 |url-status=live }}</ref>
In 1871, Bateman and his sons (who included the painter [[Robert Bateman (artist)|Robert Bateman]]) gave up the house and gardens at Biddulph, and he moved to [[Kensington]] in London. He later moved to [[Worthing]] in Sussex, where he died on 27 November 1897.{{sfn|Carlyle|1901}}

===Collector of plants===
"MA Magdalen College, Oxford, 1845, took great interest in collecting and cultivating tropical plants; FLS, 1833; FRS, 1838; fellow of Royal Horticultural Society; published writings on orchids and other horticultural subjects."<ref>''Concise Dictionary of National Biography,'' Oxford, 1995, p.169</ref>

He was a collector and scholar of [[orchids]], President of the North Staffordshire Field Society, and served on the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s Plant Exploration Committee.  He especially loved [[rhododendron]]s and [[azalea]]s. He had a number of sons who grew up at Biddulph Grange, including the painter [[Robert Bateman (artist)|Robert Bateman]].

The naturalist, Charles Darwin "received a box of orchids from Bateman on 25 January 1862 (and) a letter from him dated 28 January 1862."<ref name="Darwin">[http://www.darwinproject.ac.uk/darwinletters/calendar/entry-3356.html Darwin Correspondence Project – Letter 3356 — Bateman, James to Darwin, C. R., [1862]<!-- Bot generated title -->]. {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070927065916/http://www.darwinproject.ac.uk/darwinletters/calendar/entry-3356.html |date=27 September 2007 }}</ref>

===Garden designer===

Bateman created the gardens at Biddulph with the aid of his botanist wife Maria and his friend and painter of seascapes [[Edward William Cooke]].<ref>{{Cite book|last=Horwood|first=Catherine|title=Gardening Women: Their Stories From 1600 to the Present|publisher=Hachette, UK|year=2010|isbn=978-0748118335|location=United Kingdom|pages=94–95}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last=Musgrave|first=Toby|title=Seven deadly sins of gardening : and the vices and virtues of gardeners|last2=Calnan|first2=Mike|publisher=National Trust|year=2006|isbn=978-1-905400-46-1|location=London|pages=127–130|oclc=70173987}}</ref> His gardens at Biddulph are a rare survival of the interim period between [[Capability Brown]] [[landscape garden]] and the High [[Victorian era|Victorian]] style. The gardens are compartmentalised and divided into themes.

He "was also responsible for laying out the Arboretum at [[Derby]], the first public park in England."<ref>[http://www.francisfrith.com/search/england/staffordshire/biddulph/biddulph.htm Biddulph photos, maps, books, memories – Francis Frith] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070926231205/http://www.francisfrith.com/search/england/staffordshire/biddulph/biddulph.htm |date=26 September 2007 }}</ref>

=== Geology and religion ===

{{main|Geological Gallery, Biddulph Grange}}

[[File:The Geological Gallery, Biddulph Grange.jpg|thumb|center|upright=1.5<!--fmt for low img-->|The [[Geological Gallery, Biddulph Grange]], from the door. The bays, with a sequence of rocks below and a selection of fossils from the same [[geological era]]s above, represent the six days of [[biblical creation]].]]

Bateman expressed his strong religious beliefs in the [[Geological Gallery, Biddulph Grange|Geological Gallery at Biddulph Grange]]. Realising that a long sequence of rocks and fossils implied a great expanse of time before the supposed date of the creation of the world, he opened the gallery, a long straight corridor with specimens from oldest to youngest in sequence, to set out his view that the rocks were created by God in six days.<ref>{{cite web |title=Biddulph Grange Gardens |url=https://www.congleton-tc.gov.uk/attraction/biddulph-grange-gardens/ |publisher=Congleton Town Council |access-date=9 November 2026}}</ref><ref name="Historic England">{{cite web |title=Geological Gallery & (Site of) Orangery, Biddulph Grange |url=https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/heritage-gateway/results/record/c30a9cd9-4500-41f0-acda-ed2a4d72a681/MNA183731 |publisher=[[Historic England]] |id=MNA183731 |access-date=9 November 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Things to see in Biddulph Grange Garden: Geological Gallery |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/visit/shropshire-staffordshire/biddulph-grange-garden/things-to-see-at-biddulph-grange-garden#rt-geological-gallery |publisher=[[National Trust]] |access-date=10 November 2026}}</ref>

===Family===
On 24 April 1838, he married Maria Sybilla, third daughter of Rowland Egerton Warburton and sister of [[Peter Egerton Warburton]]; they had three sons, [[John Bateman (British politician)|John]], Rowland, and [[Robert Bateman (artist)|Robert]] (a notable painter), and a daughter, Katherine.{{sfn|Carlyle|1901}}

[[Macintosh Quadra 660AV]] | successor = [[Power Macintosh 6200]] | related = {{Unbulleted list | [[Power Macintosh 7100]] | [[Power Macintosh 8100]] | [[Workgroup Server 9150]] }} }} The '''Power Macintosh 6100''' (also sold as the '''Macintosh Performa 6110''' series and the '''Workgroup Server 6150''') is a [[personal computer]] designed, manufactured, and sold by [[Apple Computer]] from March 1994 to March 1996. It was the first Macintosh to use a [[PowerPC]] processor, developed by the [[AIM alliance]] of Apple, [[IBM]], and [[Motorola]]. The computer used a [[Pizza-box form factor|pizza-box]] case derived from the [[Macintosh Quadra 610|Centris/Quadra 610]] and [[Macintosh Quadra 660AV|660AV]].{{cite web |url=http://apple-history.com/6100 |title=Power Macintosh 6100 |website=Apple-History.com |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120107035858/http://www.apple-history.com/6100 |archive-date=January 7, 2012}} It replaced the [[Macintosh Quadra]] line of computers based on the [[Motorola 68040]]. For the consumer market, Apple sold the computer as the [[Macintosh Performa]] 6110, 6112, 6115, 6117, and 6118, with model numbers distinguishing bundled software and hard drive configurations.{{cite web |url=http://lowendmac.com/1994/power-mac-6100/ |title=Power Mac 6100 |website=Low End Mac |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180317112239/http://lowendmac.com/1994/power-mac-6100/ |archive-date=March 17, 2018}} These configurations were bundled with an [[Apple Multiple Scan 15 Display]] and an [[Apple Keyboard#AppleDesign Keyboard|AppleDesign Keyboard]]. Apple also offered the [[Apple Workgroup Server]] 6150, a server configuration that included additional server software. The Power Macintosh 6100 was discontinued in March 1996 without a direct replacement. ==Overview== The 6100 was introduced alongside the [[Power Macintosh 7100]] and [[Power Macintosh 8100]] and occupied the entry-level role of the new [[Power Macintosh]] family. ''MacWorld''{{'}}s review of the 6100/60 noted that "Not only has Apple finally regained the performance lead it lost about eight years ago when PCs appeared using Intel's 80386 CPU, but it has pushed far ahead."{{cite magazine |last=Gruman |first=Galen |date=June 1994 |title=Power Macintosh 6100/60 |url=https://archive.org/stream/MacWorld_9406_June_1994#page/n57/mode/2up |magazine=[[Macworld|MacWorld Magazine]] |pages=56–57}} Performance of 680x0 software is slower due to the need for System 7.5's new [[Mac 68k emulator|Mac 68k emulation]] layer, but ''MacWorld''{{'}}s benchmarks showed noticeably faster CPU, disk, video and floating point performance than the Quadra 610 it replaced. The 60 MHz models were upgraded to 66 MHz in January 1995.{{cite book |last1=Pogue |first1=David |title=MacWorld Mac Secrets, 5th Edition |last2=Schorr |first2=Joseph |date=1999 |publisher=[[IDG Books]] |isbn=0-7645-4040-8 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/macworldmacsecre00pogu/page/512 512-513] |chapter=Chapter 13: The PowerPC Macs, Model by Model |chapter-url=https://archive.org/details/macworldmacsecre00pogu/page/512}} The 6100 was the slowest Power Macintosh in terms of processor speed upon introduction. Eventually, the 6100 series was able to be upgraded through third-party solutions such as Sonnet Technologies' Crescendo G3 NuBus (up to 500 MHz) and G4 NuBus (up to 360 MHz; discontinued) and [[Newer Technology]]'s MaxPower G3 processor upgrades; these upgrades usually plugged into the NuBus/PDS slots of the 6100 or via the L2 cache slot (like with all other Macintoshes up until the iMac G3). These upgrades also allowed the 6100 to unofficially run up to Mac OS 9.2.2 via third-party programs such as "OS9 Helper". Notable to this generation of machines were the new startup and "[[Macintosh startup#Sad Mac|Sad Mac]]" chimes: instead of the electronic "chuff" that was used on the previous generation machines, it played a guitar chord strummed by jazz guitarist [[Stanley Jordan]], and instead of the "[[Macintosh startup#Chimes of Death|Chimes of Death]]" 8-note arpeggio that played whenever there was a hardware error at startup, there was the sound of a car crashing. Apple also released a PC-compatible model of the 6100/66 called the Power Macintosh 6100 [[DOS]] Compatible. This version came with a [[DOS Compatibility Card]] installed in the [[processor direct slot]] with an [[i486|Intel 80486]] DX2/66 processor (without L2 cache) and a single [[SIMM]] RAM slot that uses the same type of RAM as in the 6100 itself. The card supported up to 32 MB of RAM, a [[Creative Technology]] [[Sound Blaster 16#Sound Blaster VIBRA 16|Sound Blaster VIBRA 16]] sound chipset, and also included standard PC [[Video Graphics Array|VGA]] and [[Game port|joystick]] ports. With this card, the 6100 is capable of running both the Mac OS interface and DOS/[[Windows 3.1x|Windows 3.1]] side-by-side, even on different monitors. The card could also use the main system RAM if there was no SIMM installed on the card. This and the other [[NuBus]]-based Power Macintosh models ([[Power Macintosh 7100|7100]], [[Power Macintosh 8100|8100]] and [[Workgroup Server 9150]]) were replaced by the Power Macintosh [[Peripheral Component Interconnect|PCI]] series released in 1995, although the 6100 DOS Compatible model continued in production until 1996. By this time, Apple had already released the highly anticipated "PC Personality Card" that plugged into one of the PCI slots of the newer Power Macs, featuring a 100 MHz [[Pentium (original)|Pentium]] processor. Early models had a CD eject button that would stick in. This was rectified on later models with a subtly re-profiled button moulding. ==Models== The original Power Macintosh 6100 is based on the 60 MHz PowerPC 601 processor.[http://www.everymac.com/systems/apple/powermac/specs/powermac_6100_60.html Power Macintosh 6100/60 (PC) Specs] EveryMac.com." EveryMac. N.p., n.d. Web. November 23, 2012 {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130103030701/http://www.everymac.com/systems/apple/powermac/specs/powermac_6100_60.html |date=January 3, 2013 }}>. The base model was complemented by an AV version, which included an add-on card fitted in its [[Processor Direct Slot]] that added audio and visual enhancements such as [[composite video|composite]] and [[S-video]] input/output and full 48 kHz 16-bit [[Digital Audio Tape|DAT]]-resolution sound processing. A double-speed [[CD-ROM]] is included as standard. A series of Performa models based on the 6100/60 were shipped in October 1994, collectively known as the "Performa 6100 series."{{cite magazine |last=Crotty |first=Cameron |date=December 1994 |title=Power Macs Join Performa Family |url=https://archive.org/stream/MacWorld_9412_December_1994#page/n35/mode/2up |magazine=MacWorld Magazine |pages=34–35}} All Performas included an [[Apple Multiple Scan 15 Display]], an [[Apple Keyboard#AppleDesign Keyboard (M2980)|AppleDesign Keyboard]], and a suite of pre-installed software including [[Quicken]], [[MacLinkPlus]], [[The American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language|American Heritage Dictionary]], and Apple's [[eWorld]] online service. CD-ROMs included with all Performas included Electronic Arts' 3D World Atlas and a variety of software for children. The Performas vary only in their hard drive size and which of two software bundles are included. '''Software bundle 1''': [[ClarisWorks]], clip art collections, and [[Now Software]]'s Up-To-Date and Contact.
'''Software bundle 2''': [[Microsoft Works]], ''[[Mavis Beacon Teaches Typing]]'', Kid Works, ''[[Thinkin' Things]]'', The Writing Center, Fractal Dabbler, Spaceway 2000, San Diego Zoo Presents... the Animals!, [[Wacky Jacks]] CD Gameshow. The '''''North Shore Times''''' is an Australian local newspaper, that serves the [[Local government in Australia|local government areas]] of [[City of Willoughby|Willoughby]], [[Ku-ring-gai Council|Ku-ring-gai]], [[Municipality of Lane Cove|Lane Cove]] and part of [[North Sydney Council|North Sydney]]. The newspaper was launched on 11 May 1960 by a 29-year-old [[Rupert Murdoch]], making it the only other Australian newspaper started completely from scratch by Murdoch prior to his founding of ''[[The Australian]]'' in 1964.<ref>{{cite news |last=Jackson |first=Sally |title=Murdoch's The North Shore Times turns 50 |url=https://www.theaustralian.com.au/business/media/murdochs-the-north-shore-times-turns-50/news-story/bc75035a49551c9fa19db39b43745627 |work=The Australian |date=17 May 2010 |access-date=10 November 2026 |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

The paper is one of [[News Corp Australia]]'s community newspapers in [[Sydney]]. It is delivered free to homes and businesses every Thursday, as of July 2016 after originally being a Wednesday and Friday publication. The Wednesday publication was established in 1960 and the Friday publication was established in 1989.

Originally established as a Wednesday-only publication in 1960, a secondary Friday edition was introduced in 1989. It remained a bi-weekly publication for nearly three decades until July 2016, when News Corp consolidated the two editions into a single, comprehensive Thursday print publication. Reflecting broader consolidation trends across metropolitan community media, the administrative and editorial coordination of the paper was eventually moved out of the local coverage area to News Corp's major suburban hub in Parramatta.

During the May 2020 print media restructuring brought on by the [[COVID-19 pandemic]], where News Corp Australia ceased the print editions of over 100 regional and community titles, the ''North Shore Times'' was one of only three affluent Sydney community publications selected to preserve its print format due to robust local real estate advertising revenue.<ref>{{cite news |last=Meade |first=Amanda |title=News Corp announces end of more than 100 Australian print newspapers in huge shift to digital |url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2020/may/28/news-corp-announces-end-of-nearly-100-australian-print-newspapers-in-huge-shift-to-digital |work=The Guardian |date=28 May 2020 |access-date=10 November 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=News Corp cuts: Will your local newspaper be affected? |url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/2020-05-28/news-corp-cuts-is-your-local-paper-affected/12295320 |publisher=ABC News |date=28 May 2020 |access-date=10 November 2026}}</ref>

==Readership==
The circulation of both the Wednesday and Friday publications of the North Shore Times reaches approximately 75,000 homes and businesses, with the estimated total number of people who read the newspaper being around 112,000. The majority of North Shore Times' readers are in the 35–49 and 50–64 age groups.<ref>{{Cite web |last=| first= |date=June 2005 |url=http://www.community.newsmedianet.com.au/home/groups/group/title.jsp?titleid=13  |title=North Shore Times (Wed) |pages= |access-date=10 November 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050615160107/http://www.community.newsmedianet.com.au/home/groups/group/title.jsp?titleid=13 |archive-date=15 June 2005 |publisher=community.newsmedianet.com.au |work=North Shore Times }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=| first= |date=June 2005 |url=http://www.community.newsmedianet.com.au/home/groups/group/title.jsp?titleid=103 |title=North Shore Times (Fri) |pages= |access-date=10 November 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050615160020/http://www.community.newsmedianet.com.au/home/groups/group/title.jsp?titleid=103 |archive-date=15 June 2005 |publisher=community.newsmedianet.com.au |work=North Shore Times }}</ref>

== Notable editors ==
Several journalists and media professionals have served editorial roles at the ''North Shore Times'', including:
* '''Billy Cantwell''' – Editor of the ''North Shore Times'' from 2015 to 2019, who later became the Opinion Editor at ''The Sydney Morning Herald''.<ref>{{cite news |title=North Shore Times reveals mag-nificent new layout |url=https://www.dailytelegraph.com.au/newslocal/north-shore/north-shore-times-reveals-magnificent-new-layout/news-story/d0c274e9216c59008d37b25ddd2e65a2 |work=The Daily Telegraph |date=18 August 2017 |access-date=10 November 2026}}</ref>
* '''Tim McIntyre''' – Editor of the ''North Shore Times'' and the ''Mosman Daily'' from 2018 to 2019, who was later appointed as a Content Director for News Corp Australia's community publications.<ref>{{cite news |last=Meade |first=Amanda |title=Local news to return in print |url=https://www.theaustralian.com.au/business/media/news-corps-sydney-community-newspapers-return-to-print/news-story/ebe69b14f64a61f0522e58fb2b729ddf |work=The Australian |date=17 June 2020 |access-date=10 November 2026 |url-access=subscription}}</ref>
* '''Kelly Baker''' – Lifestyle journalist and television commentator who served as the Acting Editor of the masthead in June 2020 during its print transition.<ref>{{cite web |last=Baker |first=Kelly |title=Interview with Kelly Baker – Acting Editor and Arts & Lifestyle Editor |url=https://www.medianet.com.au/blog/kelly-baker |website=Medianet |date=18 June 2020 |access-date=10 November 2026}}</ref>

'''Khor Rori''' ({{langx|ar|خور روري|translit=Khawr Rawrī}}) is a [[shoal|bar]]-built [[estuary]] at the [[river mouth|mouth]] of Wādī Darbāt in the [[Dhofar Governorate]], [[Oman]], near [[Taqah]]. It is an intermittently closed/open [[lake]]/[[lagoon]], with an inlet from [[Arabian Sea]] that is usually disconnected.<ref name="Hoorn & Cremaschi">{{Cite journal|last1=Hoorn|first1=Carina|last2=Cremaschi|first2=Mauro|date=2004-10-07|title=Late Holocene palaeoenvironmental history of Khawr Rawri and Khawr Al Balid (Dhofar, Sultanate of Oman)|url=http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0031018204001865|journal=Palaeogeography, Palaeoclimatology, Palaeoecology|language=en|volume=213|issue=1|pages=1–36|doi=10.1016/j.palaeo.2004.03.014|bibcode=2004PPP...213....1H |issn=0031-0182|url-access=subscription}}</ref> It is a major breeding ground for birds,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://omantourism.gov.om/wps/portal/mot/tourism/oman/details/!ut/p/a0/04_Sj9CPykssy0xPLMnMz0vMAfGjzOItvc1dg40MzAz8Tc0NDTyDAwINvF19DN0DzPULsh0VAek2Ufo!/?WCM_GLOBAL_CONTEXT=/wps/wcm/connect/mot_english_lib/mot/media+center/press+releases/dhofar+beckons+lovers+of+nature+tourism|title=Dhofar beckons lovers of nature tourism|publisher=Ministry of Tourism (Oman)|date=29 June 2011|access-date=26 November 2019}}{{Dead link|date=June 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> and used to act as an important harbour for [[frankincense]] trade when it was an open estuary.<ref name="Hoorn & Cremaschi" /> The area represents a popular tourist spot within Oman and since 2000, is a part of the [[UNESCO]] [[World Heritage Site]], the [[Land of Frankincense]].<ref>{{Cite web|date=2000|title=Land of Frankincense|url=https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1010/|access-date=2021-03-25|website=UNESCO World Heritage Centre}}</ref>

== Overview ==
Khor Rori is best known for the ruins of the ancient fortified port city of '''Sumhuram''' on the eastern bank, which was founded in the 3rd century BC as an outpost for the [[Kingdom of Hadhramaut|Kingdom of Ḥaḍramawt]].<ref name="Avanzini & Sedov">{{Cite journal|last1=Avanzini|first1=Alessandra|last2=Sedov|first2=Alexander V.|date=2005|title=The stratigraphy of Sumhuram: new evidence|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/41219365|journal=Proceedings of the Seminar for Arabian Studies|volume=35|pages=11–17|jstor=41219365|issn=0308-8421}}</ref> After the eclipse of Ḥaḍramawt, Sumhuram was under the influence of the [[Kingdom of Ḥimyar]], as indicated by the Himyarite coins excavated from there.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Sedov|first=Alexander V.|title=A Port in Arabia Between Rome and the Indian Ocean, 3rd C.BC-5th C.AD: Khor Rori Report 2|publisher=L'Erma di Bretschneider|year=2008|isbn=978-88-8265-469-6|editor-last=Avanzini|editor-first=Alessandra|location=Rome, Italy|pages=277–316|chapter=The Coins from Sumhuram: the 2001A-2004A Seasons|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=H-pGsZR1wkcC&pg=PA283}}</ref> It was finally abandoned in the 5th century, most likely due to the formation of the sandbar blocking the estuary.<ref name="Hoorn & Cremaschi" /><ref>{{Cite book|last=Avanzini|first=Alessandra|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=H-pGsZR1wkcC&pg=PA9|title=A Port in Arabia Between Rome and the Indian Ocean, 3rd C.BC-5th C.AD: Khor Rori Report 2|publisher=L'Erma di Bretschneider|year=2008|isbn=978-88-8265-469-6|location=Rome, Italy}}</ref>

There are also archaeological ruins on the two [[promontories]] at the mouth of Khor Rori. The eastern promontory ('''Inqitat Mirbat'''<ref name="Avanzini & Orazi" />) is better explored than the western promontory ('''Inqitat Taqah'''<ref name="Avanzini & Orazi">{{Cite journal|last1=Avanzini|first1=Alessandra|last2=Orazi|first2=Roberto|date=2001|title=The construction phases of Khor Rori's monumental gate|url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1034/j.1600-0471.2001.d01-9.x|journal=Arabian Archaeology and Epigraphy|language=en|volume=12|issue=2|pages=249–259|doi=10.1034/j.1600-0471.2001.d01-9.x|issn=1600-0471|url-access=subscription}}</ref>).<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Zarins|first=Juris|date=2009|editor-last=Avanzini|editor-first=Allesandra|title=The Latest on the Archaeology of Southern Oman|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/25766909|journal=Journal of the American Oriental Society|volume=129|issue=4|pages=665–674|jstor=25766909|issn=0003-0279}}</ref> Inqitat Mirbat, also known as '''Khatiya''' or '''al-Ḥamr al-Sharqiya''',<ref name="Bent" /><ref name="Rougeulle">{{Cite book|last=Rougeulle|first=Axelle|title=A Port in Arabia Between Rome and the Indian Ocean, 3rd C.BC-5th C.AD: Khor Rori Report 2|publisher=L'Erma di Bretschneider|year=2008|isbn=978-88-8265-469-6|editor-last=Avanzini|editor-first=Alessandra|location=Rome, Italy|pages=645–667|chapter=A Medieval Trade Entrepôt at Khor Rori? The Study of the Islamic Ceramic from al-Ḥamr al-Sharqiya|chapter-url=https://halshs.archives-ouvertes.fr/halshs-00357676/document}}</ref> had been inhabited by the 4th century BC before the emergence of Sumhuram, and its settlement history might date back to the 8th century BC.<ref name="Lischi">{{Cite book|last=Lischi|first=Silvia|title=South Arabian Long-Distance Trade in Antiquity: "Out of Arabia"|date=2021-02-01|publisher=Cambridge Scholars Publishing|isbn=978-1-5275-6533-3|editor-last=Hatke|editor-first=George|pages=228–244|chapter=Notes on the South Arabian Occupation of Inqitat|editor-last2=Ruzicka|editor-first2=Ronald|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UEcdEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA228}}</ref> It was abandoned in the 1st or 2nd century,<ref name="Lischi" /> and re-occupied in the medieval period.<ref name="Rougeulle" />

==History==
Inscriptions at Khor Rori report that the town of Sumhuram (Hadramautic: s<sup>1</sup>mhrm), was founded on royal initiative and settled by Hadhrami emigrants. The Dhofar region was the main source of [[frankincense]] in the ancient period, and it seems likely that the foundation of the settlement by the Hadhramaut was in part motivated by wish to control the production of this valuable commodity.

Khor Rori has been tentatively identified as the location of '''Moscha Limen''' ({{langx|grc|Μόσχα λιμήν}}, probably meaning "the harbour of young shoots (μόσχος)" and referring to the possible [[mangrove]] vegetation in the past,<ref>{{Cite book|last=Bukharin|first=Mikhail|title=Khor Rori Report 1|publisher=Edizioni Plus|year=2002|isbn=88-8492-031-0|editor-last=Avanzini|editor-first=Alessandra|location=Pisa, Italy|pages=323–324|chapter=The Name of Moscha Limen|chapter-url=https://www.academia.edu/8666217}}</ref> or else "the harbour of ''musk''/perfume"<ref name=Schoff>[[Wilfred Harvey Schoff]], ''The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea: travel and trade in the Indian Ocean'', (Longmans, Green, and Co., 1912) [https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Page:The_Periplus_of_the_Erythr%C3%A6an_Sea.djvu/153 p. 140-143]</ref>). The name appeared in the anonymous ''[[Periplus of the Erythraean Sea]]'' of the 1st century CE, and in [[Ptolemy]]'s ''[[Geographia]]'' in the next century. It has also been identified with '''Abissa polis''' or '''Abyssapolis''' ({{langx|grc|Ἄβισσα πόλις}}) from Ptolemy; this name has first been connected with the ''abyss'' besides the waterfall of Wādī Darbāt,<ref name="Bent">{{Cite journal|last=Bent|first=James Theodore|date=1895|title=Exploration of the Frankincense Country, Southern Arabia |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1773739|journal=The Geographical Journal|volume=6|issue=2|pages=109–133|doi=10.2307/1773739|jstor=1773739|bibcode=1895GeogJ...6..109B |issn=0016-7398|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Bent|first=James Theodore|date=1895|title=The Land of Frankincense and Myrrh|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nRADAAAAIAAJ&pg=PA595|journal=The Nineteenth Century|volume=38|issue=224|pages=595–613}}</ref><ref name="Mr. & Mrs. Bent">{{Cite book|last1=Bent|first1=James Theodore|title=Southern Arabia|last2=Bent|first2=Mabel Virginia Anna|publisher=Smith, Elder & Co.|year=1900|location=London, England|pages=268–276|chapter=The Identification of Abyssapolis|chapter-url=https://archive.org/details/southernarabia00bentuoft/page/268/mode/2up}}</ref> but may be related to the [[Abyssinia]]n people.<ref name=Schoff/><ref name="Breyer">{{cite journal |last1=Breyer |first1=Francis |title=The Ancient Egyptian Etymology of Ḥabašāt "Abessinia" |journal=Ityop̣is |date=2016 |volume=Extra Issue II |pages=8–18 |url=http://www.ityopis.org/Issues-Extra-2_files/ityopis-extra2-breyer.pdf |quote=The forms with <y> are an academic “Volksetymologie” (comp. Gr. ἄβυσσος “Abyss”).}}</ref> The existence of an ancient port city in this area has been expected by 19th century western geographers based on the classical and Arabic sources. In the 1890s the location was pointed out by [[Eduard Glaser]], and English explorer [[James Theodore Bent]], who visited it in January 1895 with his wife [[Mabel Bent|Mabel]], published a description of it, and reiterated the double identification.<ref name="Mr. & Mrs. Bent" /><ref name="Bent" />

In 1908, [[John Gordon Lorimer (1870-1914)|J.G. Lorimer]] recorded Khor Rori in his ''[[Gazetteer of the Persian Gulf, Oman and Central Arabia|Gazetteer of the Persian Gulf]]'', noting its location as the eastern extremity of Dhofar proper. He wrote:
{{Blockquote|A remarkable lake or inlet of the sea running a mile or more inland; it is the estuary of Wadi Dirbat from Jabal Samhan.

The inlet is divided from the sea by a sand bar over which the water flows at high tide. A peninsula, once fortified, adjoins the east side of the entrance. Remains of ancient buildings surround the lake. There is a fortified rock at the entrance to the inlet, which is called Khatiyah. This harbour is the ancient Moscha, or Abyssapolis.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.qdl.qa/en/archive/81055/vdc_100023909213.0x0000aa|title='Gazetteer of Arabia Vol. I' [538] (569/1050)|date=22 October 2014 |publisher=Qatar Digital Library|access-date=26 November 2019}} ''This article incorporates text from this source, which is in the [[public domain]].''</ref> }}

The site has been excavated by the American Foundation for the Study of Man (AFSM) in the early 1950s<ref>{{cite journal |last=Breton |first=Jean-François |date=2009 |title=Alessandra AVANZINI éd., ''Khor Rori Report 1''. (review) |journal=[[Syria (journal)|Syria]] |volume=86 |pages=369–370 |doi=10.4000/syria.594 |doi-access=free |language=fr}}</ref> and by the Italian Mission to Oman (IMTO) since 1996.<ref>{{Cite journal |title=Ancient Arabia: archaeology & history of pre-islamic Arabia |url=https://ancientarabia.huma-num.fr/dictionary/definition/khawr-ruri-ancient-sumhuram |language=en |doi=10.60667/tdaa-0070}}</ref> The excavations have uncovered the ground plan of the settlement and has attested maritime contacts with the Ḥaḑramite homeland, India and the Mediterranean.{{cn|date=September 2026}}

It was inscribed in 2000, along with other sites along the [[Incense Route]] in Oman, as part of the [[World Heritage Site]] "[[Land of Frankincense]]".<ref>{{cite journal |last=Ray |first=Himanshu Prabha |date=September 2020 |title=Culture and Diplomacy: Maritime Cultural Heritage of the Western Indian Ocean |journal=[[India Quarterly]] |volume=76 |issue=3 |pages=375–391 |doi=10.1177/0974928420936112 |jstor=48589422}}</ref>{{rp|384}}

== Trade ==
The Dhofar region produced two types of frankincense: carfiathum and dathiathum. Carfiathum is regarded as the superior frankincense to dathiathum. Frankincense was collected in seasonal cycles, carfiathum in the fall and dathiathum in the spring, enabling some degree of year-round commercial activities.<ref>{{Cite book |last=de Romanis |first=F. |title=Along the aroma and spice routes The harbour of Sumhuram, its territory and the trade between the Mediterranean, Arabia and India |publisher=Bandecchi & Vivaldi |year=2011 |pages=120–121 |chapter=Commercial Activity at Moscha limén}}</ref>

Supposedly, Egyptian and Indian goods were traded at Sumhuram in exchange for frankincense. Some scholars have argued that bronze was imported to Moscha Limen from Egypt and used to create coins. Sumhuram is believed to have been a center of coin manufacturing as suggested by the copious amounts of bronze coins found at the site, excavated structures that resemble known warehouses from nearby cities, and trade documentation from the ''Periplus.''<ref>Avanzini, A.; Pavan, A. (2011). "Sumhuram, a South Arabian port". ''Along the aroma and spice routes The harbour of Sumhuram, its territory and the trade between the Mediterranean, Arabia and India''. Bandecchi & Vivaldi. pp. 44–46.</ref><ref>D’Andrea, C. Tavolieri. (2011). "Sumhuram in the classical sources". ''Along the aroma and spice routes The harbour of Sumhuram, its territory and the trade between the Mediterranean, Arabia and India''. Bandecchi & Vivaldi. pp. 118.</ref>
==Other contexts==
In tourism literature, Sumhuram is occasionally promoted as the summer palace of the [[Queen of Sheba]],<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Kessler|first1=Kristel|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=KeWCDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA131|title=Islamic Tourism: Management of Travel Destinations|last2=Raj|first2=Razaq|publisher=CABI|year=2018|isbn=978-1-78639-413-2|editor-last=Jamal|editor-first=Ahmad|location=Boston, MA|pages=131|language=en|chapter=Religious Tourism in the Sultanate of Oman: The Potential for Mosque Tourism to Thrive|editor-last2=Griffin|editor-first2=Kevin|editor-last3=Raj|editor-first3=Razaq}}</ref> the legendary ruler of the [[Sabaeans|Sabaʾ Kingdom]] living in the 10th century BC.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Queen of Sheba|url=https://www.britannica.com/biography/Queen-of-Sheba|access-date=2021-03-23|website=Encyclopedia Britannica}}</ref>

Some members of [[the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints]] believe that Khor Rori is the "[[Bountiful (Book of Mormon)|land Bountiful]]" where [[Nephi, son of Lehi|Nephi]] from the [[Book of Mormon]] stayed during his travels from Jerusalem ([[First Nephi]], chapter 17).<ref>Potter, George and Wellington, Richard. ''Lehi's Trail: From the Valley of Lemuel to Nephi's Harbor.http://maxwellinstitute.byu.edu/publications/jbms/?vol=15&num=2&id=415''</ref>

However, current archaeological evidence indicates that Sumhuram was founded in the 3rd century BC by the [[Kingdom of Hadhramaut|Kingdom of Ḥaḍramawt]].<ref name="Avanzini & Sedov" />
